tasks.title: T-C3-01 (P5, low) — C3: 17 of the 50 comment-versus-code sites remain — 33 fixed, and this card is the resume point
tasks.description:
Summary
    The comment-versus-code audit found 50 places where a comment describes something the code does not do. 33 are fixed and this card is where the remaining 17 are picked up.

Done so far
    33 sites across 9 files, in 11 commits from `ddec417` to `80a244d` — 144 insertions, 125 deletions. The files: `TurboMCPKitCommandlet.cpp` (14 sites), `GraphFixBackward.cpp` (the capped-list count), `Capture.cpp` (two refusals that began with the banner), `MaterialBlocks.cpp` (five false promises of a title or a check), `Material.cpp` (a dead counter and two histories), `Toolsets.h` (an over-promise of verification), plus `GraphFixBackward.h`, `GraphTidy.cpp` and `GraphTidy.h`.

First action
    Nothing here has been compiled yet. Build before anything else, and build the whole target rather than incrementally: `FPlan` gained a field in `GraphFixBackward.h` and lost one in `GraphTidy.h`.

Two findings diagnosed but not applied
    1. `GraphKnots.cpp:1329` — `MarkPackageDirty()` runs before the rollback decision, so a pass that rolls back leaves the package dirty and the editor offers to save a change that does not exist. The obvious fix is wrong: moving the call does not clear the flag, and clearing it blindly throws away a dirty state that may belong to something else. The fix is three lines with a `bWasDirty` captured before the first write. This needs a compile, not more reading.
    2. `Struct.cpp:1534` — the earlier card was wrong twice. The rename failure *is* reported (`Vanished.Add` plus `continue`, and `++Added` is skipped), and `:1550` cannot write to a pre-existing field because `GuidOfField` matches on `FriendlyName` and the field was never renamed. The real defect is that `MakeUniqueFriendlyName` and `AddVariable` have already run, so the struct gains a field under an unrequested name while the report says the field did not arrive. Whether that branch is reachable at all needs a run: call `E-STRUCT-ADD` twice on one name and read the field list back. The kit commandlet already builds a user struct, so the fixture exists.

What remains
    `GraphKnots.cpp:1334` (the `>=` rather than `>` rollback test, to be read with the branch it guards), two more sites in `Struct.cpp`, one more in `GraphKnots.cpp`, and five files with one or two sites each, named by line number further down this card's original notes.

Already checked and correct — do not re-read
    `Struct.cpp:183` (a deliberate engine exception, `PC_Real` accepting `PC_Int`), `KitCommandlet.cpp:639`, `:832`, `:1483`, `GraphFixBackward.cpp:90` (the fallback flag *is* set at `:719` and read at `:1645`; the `:716` the old card cited is a `return;` in a different file), `Capture.cpp:906`, `Toolsets.h:1958` (`GraphReplace` does carry a title), `Toolsets.h:37`, `:410`, `:1174`, `:1244`, `Material.cpp:1450` (`; error:` is an established inline convention, documented at `BlueprintJson.cpp:183` and `GraphLoad.cpp:144`) and `Material.cpp:160`.

The shapes behind the 50 sites
    24 sites are a comment describing an intention the code never implemented — fix the comment. 3 sites are code breaching a rule the file itself states — both in `Capture.cpp`, fix the code. 5 of the 8 code defects are a field written once and read nowhere, sitting beside a comment that claims it is reported — remove the field or make it real.

Note
    The third shape cannot be found by a script, and that was tested rather than assumed: `Tools/checks/check-dead-fields.py` was written for it, ran, and returned 254 candidates with none of the three real cases among them, because they are locals rather than struct fields. `80a244d` records that failure inside the tool. Verifying each site before changing it is the larger half of this work — six of the 33 sites turned out to be cards that were simply wrong, and two of those proposed a fix that would have broken something.

tasks.title: T-METHOD-01 (P3, medium) — Every count in every card must state the scope it was taken over — 161 is a floor, not a total
tasks.description:
Summary
    A count was published from an estimate and then measured. The mechanism named first was wrong; the conclusion is the same and the numbers are now real. The rule this card leaves behind: every count must state the scope it was taken over.

What was claimed, and why it was wrong
    The first version said 68 of 99 reports survived and 31 were lost, because the workflow caps each report at 3,500 characters and a truncated report can lose its lines from the tail. The cap is real — it was set by hand in the workflow script — but it is not what removed the reports. The spill file holds the workflow's return value, and the tool truncates that value to fit its output limit. The 3,500-character cap affected content, not count.

What was actually measured
    `src-batch1-raw.txt` has 12 `FILE:` markers and 10 `FINDINGS:` lines, with 2 reports cut mid-sentence. `src-batch2-raw.txt` has 28 and 27, with 1 cut mid-sentence. So 9 of the 68 saved reports are complete-but-short rather than truncated, and the real loss is the reports the spill never carried at all: 40 audited in batch 1 with 12 saved, 59 in batch 2 with 28 saved.
    The surviving numbers are larger than the card's own figure suggested: the 10 complete batch-1 reports declare 168 findings between them — not the ~50 lines that fitted the cap — and the 27 complete batch-2 reports declare 118, which matches.

The conclusion, now measured
    "161 C3 sites" is not the total of the saved reports either. It is the total of the lines that fitted. 161 is a floor.

The lesson
    It is sharper than the first version, because the same mistake was made again inside the correction: a mechanism was named from plausibility instead of from measurement. The plausibility was good — the cap was set by hand — and it was still not the cause.

tasks.title: T-AUDIT-10 (P5, low) — AUDITED BY HAND 10/49: TurboMCPWidgetTreeText.cpp — 688 lines, one comment omits the character its sibling calls decisive, and no round-trip defect
tasks.description:
Summary
    `TurboMCPWidgetTreeText.cpp`, 688 lines — the dialect's text parser and writer, and the only file in the set with no transactions, no writes and no counters. The code patterns that dominate the material and source-control writers cannot occur here. One finding, and one suspicion checked and discarded.

What was found
    The scanner's doc comment omits the one character its own sibling calls decisive. `:89` says a bare token runs "up to whitespace, a closing parenthesis or a comment", but the code at `:96-100` also stops on `(` and on `;`. The neighbouring `IsPlainName` — the function that decides what may be written bare — names the missing case as the decisive one: a space, a parenthesis, a quote, a semicolon or a line break "would end the token early or start a comment, so those are the ones that have to be quoted". One comment is therefore complete and its neighbour is not, and they describe the same rule from the two sides of one round trip. A reader who trusts `:89` and writes a value containing `(` produces text their own parser stops short on.
    Fix: one clause — "up to whitespace, an opening or closing parenthesis, or a comment".

A suspicion that was checked and discarded
    A round-trip defect looked likely: `WriteValue` at `:118-137` emits a value bare whenever `IsPlainName` allows it, and `TakeToken` stops on `(` — so a value containing `(` would be written bare and parse short. Reading `IsPlainName` settles it: it rejects `(`, `)`, `"`, `;` and every whitespace character, so such a value is quoted and the round trip holds. There is no defect there.

What is right (do not re-investigate)
    `:35-44` explains why a scanner rather than a token array, and the reason is diagnostic quality rather than speed: the faults worth naming are positional ("unclosed parenthesis at line 12", "expected a class after `:class`"), and a scanner can say where it stopped while a pre-tokenised array has to carry a position on every token to say the same thing. All 24 diagnostics name a line — every `OutReason`/`OutError` begins `line %d:` and says what was expected and what was found (`:175`, `:186`, `:203`, `:210`, `:220`, `:257`, `:271`, `:279`, `:289`, `:299`, `:346`, `:361`, `:372`, `:383`, `:395`, `:423`, `:559`, `:575`, `:584`, `:598`, `:648`). `:117-136` escapes `;` as well as `"`, because an unescaped semicolon inside a quoted value would still be read back as the start of a comment by a reader that applied the comment rule before the quoting rule; `:159-164` honours that escape. `:118-123` writes an empty value as `""` so an empty string survives the round trip. `:56-57` returns `'\0'` at the end rather than reading past it, so callers can compare without a bounds test. `:66-69` is the only place `Line` advances, so a line number cannot drift from the position. `:73-79` treats `\r` as whitespace as well as `\n`, which is what makes a CRLF input parse.

Note
    The two defect families that account for most findings in the material writers cannot occur in a pure text transform. A defect count per file is not a measure of quality: this may be the cleanest file in the set because the shape of the work removes the opportunities, not because its author was more careful.

tasks.title: T-AUDIT-12 (P1, medium) — AUDITED BY HAND 12/49: TurboMCPOverrideRemove.cpp — 182 lines, the count that caught its worst bug is not in the answer
tasks.description:
Summary
    `TurboMCPOverrideRemove.cpp`, 182 lines — the shortest file in the set, and good code. It names the measurement that once caught its own worst bug, then does not report that measurement.

What was found
    `:88-95` records what the first version did: it called `RemoveGraph` on the event's graph, and for an event override that graph holds every other event and the whole body of the Blueprint — so removing one override destroyed the other three and the graph with them, taking the overridden count from 4 to 1. It was caught only because the count after the removal was read back and compared with the count before.
    The delivered answer carries no count. `:111-124` reads `bStillImplemented` through the editor's own list and prints "the editor now reports it as implemented: %s"; `:141-153` does the same on the function-graph path. So the one measurement credited with catching the worst defect in this file's history is not in the answer. A regression of that shape today would be caught only by `bStillImplemented` going false, which is weaker: deleting the event graph also removes the override, so it cannot tell "the override went" from "the override and three others went".
    Fix: `UBlueprintEditorLibrary::ListEvents` and `ListFunctions` are already called at `:113` and `:142`, so the before/after count is two lines away. Print it the way `TurboMCPMaterialInstance.cpp:359-365` does — "looked at %d level(s) in the chain, each for: %s".

What is right (a lot for 182 lines)
    `:71-72` names both shapes before looking for either: an event override is a node in the ubergraph and a function override is a graph of its own, and both are looked for because a caller does not know which one they made. `:80` walks the node loop backwards, which is the only safe way to destroy from a container while iterating it. `:97-103` performs the same three steps the editor's own node deletion performs (`Modify`, `DestroyNode`, `MarkPackageDirty`). `:111` does the read-back through the editor's own list, so the answer is the engine's rather than the tool's own bookkeeping. `:125` and `:154` both say the change is in memory and not saved, and to call `E-SAVE`. `:159-161` lists the overridden names when nothing matched, so a caller corrects itself in one step. `:52` and `:67` both begin with `error:` and name what is wrong.

Note
    The file uses no `FScopedTransaction` at all — the undo step is the editor's own, through `Modify()` and `DestroyNode()` — and it has no unchecked cancel. The 28 found across the tree are confined to the three material writers.

tasks.title: T-AUDIT-14 (P1, medium) — AUDITED BY HAND 14/49: TurboMCPEnumAdd.cpp — 311 lines, Renamed restates the request while ShownAs beside it is measured
tasks.description:
Summary
    `TurboMCPEnumAdd.cpp` is 311 lines. One finding: a counter that restates the request and is printed as if it were a measurement — in a block that measures its neighbour honestly.

What was found
    `:224-231` adds the enumerators, `:248-254` builds `NewNames` from `InPlan.Values` (one entry per requested value), `:276` sets `int32 Renamed = NewNames.Num()`, and `:302` prints "names set: %d". But `:301` already printed "values: %d" from the same input — the same number twice, once as the request and once as the result. Nothing reads the enum back to see whether the names landed. The read-back was available and is named in this very file: `:247` cites `GetIndexByName`, which is exactly the call that would answer it.
    The contrast is eight lines up, in the same block: `:256-274` takes `SetEnums`' bool return and refuses in words when it is false, and `:279-290` counts `ShownAs` only from setters that returned true — a genuine measurement.
    Fix: read the names back and print the count that actually landed.

A claim that was checked and discarded
    The first version of this card said `:230` ignores the return value of `AddNewEnumeratorForUserDefinedEnum`. The engine header settles it: `EnumEditorUtils.h:60` declares it `static UNREALED_API void`, so there is no result to ignore and there was no finding. The header is mixed, which is why the piste looked plausible — `:95 SetEnumeratorDisplayName` returns `bool` while `:63 RemoveEnumeratorFromUserDefinedEnum` returns `void`.

What this file gets right (do not re-investigate)
    `:233-247` records a failed reflection attempt and what it taught: `UEnum::Names` is a private union of a `const FName*` used by compiled-in enums and a `TArray` used by user-defined ones, and it carries no `UPROPERTY`, so `FindFProperty` cannot see it — the tool detected that and said so rather than writing a wrong name. `:241-243` explains why `SetEnums` is safer than poking entries: it rebuilds the name list in one step, so there is no half-renamed state to leave behind. `:245-247` keeps the engine's own name prefix, because `GenerateFullEnumName` is what the engine produces and a bare name would not resolve through `GetIndexByName`. `:260-263` notes that `EEnumFlags` is a global enum in `ObjectMacros.h` while `EAddMaxKeyIfMissing` and `EUnderlyingType` are members. `:265-273` refuses a false `SetEnums` with the cause named and still tells the caller the asset exists and is editable. `:226-227` keeps the internal `_MAX` entry in place. `:295-297` tells the asset registry, with the consequence stated.

Second file, read structurally only
    `TurboMCPWidgetBindAdd.cpp` (171 lines): the bindings array is walked backwards at `:110`, `Modify()` is called at `:116` and `:130`, and `:167` reads `Bindings.Num()` into the answer — so it has a read-back and no unchecked cancel. Its structure was read, not all 171 lines, and the card says so rather than claiming it clean.

tasks.title: T-AUDIT-16 (P5, low) — AUDITED BY HAND 16/49: TurboMCPTokenEstimate — 48 correct lines and one false universal (one finding withdrawn after checking the spec)
tasks.description:
Summary
    `TurboMCPTokenEstimate`, 48 lines. One finding was withdrawn after checking the spec; the second survives and is stronger than when it was written. The withdrawal is recorded in full so nobody files it again.

Finding withdrawn — the parameter is documented where a caller looks
    The first version of this card said `TokenBudget` is documented eight times in the header and zero times in the only published document. Checking the published specification settles it: `Spec/03_TOOLS.md:29` ("large outputs take `TokenBudget` (0 means no limit)"), `:163`, `:205` ("token budget: when the output would pass the budget, step down the detail"), and `Spec/04_FORMATS.md:190-192` ("### Budget steps"). So the parameter is documented in the tool reference and in the format specification, and `TOOLS.md`'s silence is correct and deliberate: measured, every one of its rows is a name index — a tool, one sentence, a source line — and not a reference.
    How the mistake happened, because the shape recurs: the measurement was sound and the claim built on it was not. One document was measured, then a conclusion was drawn about the documentation as a whole without opening the file whose entire subject is the tools.

Finding confirmed
    The header claims "it is an estimate, and every tool description that mentions tokens says so". Measured: no tool description in `TurboMCPToolsets.h` contains the word "estimate" or the word "token" as prose. The header uses `TokenBudget` as a parameter name and explains the cap, which is a different statement from calling the figure an estimate, and `TOOLS.md` contains neither word. The claim is a universal — "every ... says so" — and it is false. It is the shape a reader trusts precisely because it is specific. The repair is either to add the word to the descriptions or to delete the sentence; the estimate itself is correct and its own name already says what it is.

What the file gets right
    The header explains why not "characters divided by four": outputs are S-expressions rather than prose, and most punctuation costs about a token per character, so the naive rule undercounts by half and a budget built on it would let through twice what it promised — a wrong rule, the direction and size of its error, and the consequence of using it. `:22` computes `Total += (RunLength + 3) / 4;` with the identity stated so the expression is not magic. `:15-16` names the double-close before the code performs it, which is the easiest part of this pattern to get wrong. `:37-39` counts whitespace as 0 and every other visible character as 1, naming the four whitespace characters these outputs actually contain. `:46` is the second `CloseRun()` the comment promised.

Tally
    One finding withdrawn, one confirmed — and the withdrawal is the more useful of the two, because it removes work that would have been done for nothing.

tasks.title: T-AUDIT-17 (P6, low) — AUDITED BY HAND 17/49: TurboMCPPureChecks.cpp — 132 lines, zero defects, and the structural reason why
tasks.description:
Summary
    `TurboMCPPureChecks.cpp`, 132 lines, zero defects found. It is the cleanest file in the set, and the reason is reproducible rather than a matter of care.

What the file does well
    1. `:20-29` — "the echo is folded; the measurement is not". `arguments` is free text a caller wrote, so it can contain line breaks that would cut the report's line shape. `FoldedToLines` folds only the echo; the string handed to `AssetFromArguments` is the caller's original string, so the answer this tool reports is the answer the real function gives. A display fix that provably does not touch the value under test, stated in one clause.
    2. `:39-50` — an optional empty string is written so it is visible rather than absent, because a line that ends after its separator is indistinguishable from a line that failed to print, and the project has recorded that confusion as its most expensive one. The repair is doubled: `(empty)` is printed as a word, and `:121`/`:128` print the length as a number, so a caller that does not trust the word does not have to.
    3. `:100-108` — the same rule applied to the one case the tool cannot reach: "no spelling is not one key". A report that printed only `toolset distinct keys | 0` would read as a normaliser that collapsed everything, which is the opposite of what an empty input says. So it prints two lines instead: that no toolset spelling was given, and that this is an absent measurement rather than one key or zero keys.
    4. `:114-118` — the asset extraction's length is printed too, because that pure function fails silently when it is wrong: an asset name that comes back empty makes the per-asset totals quietly short with no error anywhere. The answer and its length are both printed, and the length is a number.

Smaller points worth copying
    `:63-65` accepts commas and pipes as separators, because the project's list convention admits either and a caller who uses the other should not get a silent single spelling. `:76-78` trims the echo only — a display change that provably cannot change the answer. `:110-112` prints the count, so a caller reads a number rather than deciding whether a sentence sounds like agreement. `:56-57` states its own safety as a property: it reads no log, loads no asset and writes nothing, so it needs no fixture, cannot race another suite, and has nothing to restore.

Why it has no defects
    It writes nothing, so the rollback family cannot apply. It declares no counter, so the dead-counter family cannot apply. Every optional value has `(empty)` or `(none)`, so the missing-count family cannot apply. And every claim it makes about itself is about a pure function of its inputs, which cannot drift from the code that implements it.
    The pattern across seventeen files is now clear enough to state: the defects live where a file makes a claim about something it does not control — an engine call that returns a result, a transaction that may not roll back, a list it counted itself. This file controls everything it claims about.

tasks.title: T-AUDIT-18-19 (P5, low) — AUDITED BY HAND 18-19/49: TurboMCPSettings.cpp clean; TurboMCPModule.cpp measures the analytics install and only logs it, plus a member read nowhere in the repository
tasks.description:
Summary
    Two small files read to the end. `TurboMCPSettings.cpp` (27 lines) is clean. `TurboMCPModule.cpp` (135 lines) has two confirmed findings.

What was found
    1. The analytics install is measured and then only logged. At `:121-127` the code calls `Install()`, keeps the answer in `bInstalledAnalyticsProvider`, and its only destination is a `UE_LOG` line. Nothing returns it, nothing refuses on it, no suite can observe it. The file itself explains why that matters: `:99-101` records that a missing registry is deliberately not an error when there is no editor, so a headless run installs no provider, logs "no", and passes. The measurement exists with no path from it to a failure. Fix it the way the project already does elsewhere: `TurboMCPPureChecks.cpp:114-118` prints a value *and* its length, because an asset name that comes back empty makes the per-asset totals quietly short with no error anywhere.
    2. `PreviousAnalyticsProvider` is declared, reset, and never read anywhere in the repository. `git grep` returns exactly two lines: the declaration at `TurboMCPModule.h:62` and `Reset()` at `TurboMCPModule.cpp:130`. There is no third occurrence — it is never read, tested, moved or returned. `:135-137` says why it is dead: the provider restores the one it wrapped only when it is still the one installed, so the provider owns the restore and this member is what remains of a version where the module did. Delete the member and the `Reset()`; the unconditional `Uninstall()` above them is already safe by the provider's own idempotence, which `:135-142` states.

What is right in these two files (do not re-investigate)
    `TurboMCPSettings.cpp:9-10` gives the empty constructor a reason: the defaults are declared on the members, so it exists only to give the class a body the engine can construct from config. `:16-19` distinguishes the two accessors rather than aliasing them — `GetMutableDefault` is what `UDeveloperSettings` expects, the engine creates one instance and keeps it, so the panel's checkbox cannot drift from what `SaveConfig` writes. In the module: `:17-21` justifies the registry wait by the failure it prevents (registering in `StartupModule` would leave the class unregistered with no error, and the editor looks fine); `:23-25` offers the panel early so a developer sees the honest "missing" lines; `:30-35` is the focus guard, with four measured failures behind it — four attempts from outside the process each killed the editor, because the message loop treats an externally hidden or minimised main window as a shutdown condition, and the guard does nothing unless the run is unattended; `:67-80` removes the delegate before the toolsets and the guard last, because the guard needs Slate to unhook itself; `:113-120` lists the analytics attribute names with their source and notes they are BLAKE3 hashes with no arguments, which is why the plugin's own tools write their own full-detail lines as well; `:121-124` keeps the provider that was already installed and forwards every event, so installing this cannot lose an event; `:135-142` calls `Uninstall` unconditionally, arguing from idempotence rather than a guard — and the guard-free form is the one that cannot go stale.

tasks.title: T-AUDIT-20 (P6, low) — AUDITED BY HAND 20/49: TurboMCPTraps.cpp — 202 lines, zero defects, and four failure states kept distinct
tasks.description:
Summary
    `TurboMCPTraps.cpp`, 202 lines, zero defects found. One word in one comment is optimistic, and it is recorded as the small thing it is rather than inflated into a finding.

What the file does well
    It keeps four failure states apart that most code merges into one. `:27-32` keeps the parser separate from the loader, so a parse failure and a missing file are reported differently, because they need different fixes. `:41-45` reports "the file is not valid JSON". `:48-52` reports "the file has no 'tools' object". `:97-101` reports "the file parsed but recorded no tools". And `:152-156` reports "no traps file could be read. Tried: %s" with every path, plus the error that rejected any file that existed and did not parse (`:148`). Four distinct answers, each leading to a different action, and the answer names every path it looked at.
    `:144-146` warns about a file that exists but does not parse even when an earlier file already provided notes, because the author will otherwise never learn their file is being ignored — the failure that is easiest to hide is the one this file refuses to hide. `:174-176` parses into a temporary so a broken later file cannot erase notes that an earlier file provided. `:184-186` replaces a tool's entry outright and says why: merging would make it impossible to remove a trap that no longer applies, which is argued from what the user needs to be able to do rather than from what is convenient to implement. `:191-197` builds the table once in a function-local static, which is thread safe in C++11 and matters because tool calls can arrive on a worker thread. `:122-125` adds the engine copy only when it is not the same path as the shipped one, so a project carrying its own copy does not read the same file twice. `:110-118` builds every path through `FPaths::Combine`, so no absolute machine path appears anywhere in the file.

The one thing to change
    `:109` says "shipped notes first, so a project file can add to or correct them", but `LoadFile` replaces a tool's entry outright and the comment at `:184-186` explains why. A project file can therefore correct a shipped note and cannot add one to it. The comment at `:184` is right and the one at `:109` is more optimistic than the code. One clause to fix.

tasks.title: T-AUDIT-22 (P1, medium) — AUDITED BY HAND 22/49: TurboMCPCallCostTools.cpp read to the end — a substituted cap parameter, and reporting discipline the three material writers lack
tasks.description:
Summary
    `TurboMCPCallCostTools.cpp` (403 lines) was read to the end. The first finding held; the second was too strong and is narrowed here after reading the rest of the file. The same file is also the best reporting example in the whole audit.

What was found
    1. An unreadable numeric parameter is silently replaced — the second instance of this pattern in two files. In `TurboMCPTypes.cpp:395-404` and again at `TurboMCPCallCostTools.cpp:114-122`, a value that fails to parse falls back to the default: `banana`, `0` and `-5` all produce the answer for 50 (types) or 10 (this file). A refused value and an accepted value print the same line. Fix: refuse the bad value by name, the way `TurboMCPTypes.cpp:407` now does.
    2. Narrowed: the earlier note said `FMath::Min(Wanted, 50)` "bounds silently". That was too strong. tasks.title: T-SUITE-02 (P3, low) — The FAILS ON convention measures a vocabulary, not a quality — two full suites tested, and one of the 34 silent ones is exemplary
tasks.description:
Summary
    This card's finding was tested against two full suites, and the test changed what it claims.

What was measured
    `Tools/checks/check-fails-on.py` reads 52 suites and 1546 `check()` calls: 18 name a failing input by the broad pattern, 9 by the narrow one, and 34 do not.
    `test-uncovered-tools.py` (176 lines) is one of the nine, and it also records the two wrong versions of its own checks — its best line is the best statement of the comment-versus-code problem in this audit: "the output is asserted, not the doc comment … a check written from a doc comment tests the comment."
    `test-asset-cost.py` (175 lines) is one of the 34 and it is complete. It has no `FAILS ON` line, and 14 active checks that each name what they prove: "it names soft references as their own kind", "the split states how many dependency entries were examined", "an unknown size comes with a reason rather than alone", "it says explicitly that this is not zero", "the refusal does not claim a zero size, which would read as free".

The conclusion, and why the first version of this card was wrong
    The convention measures a vocabulary, not a quality. A suite can satisfy every rule the template states and never write `FAILS ON`; a suite can write it and assert something its own author later recorded as wrong. That is exactly why the first version of this card was wrong to imply that 43 suites were defective, and why the tool now carries its own limit in its output.

The decision, with both costs measured
    Drop it: the phrase measures a comment, not a check, and `test-asset-cost.py` is the evidence — fourteen checks that state their own failure conditions without using the phrase. Removing the rule from `make-tools-doc.py` costs nothing that anything else depends on.
    Or rewrite it: "name an input that makes the check fail" is a good requirement, and `FAILS ON` is only one way of meeting it. As it stands the template asks for a sentence shape, and a sentence shape is not a property of a test.
    Recommendation: drop it, or rewrite the rule to ask for what it means. A rule that a good suite violates is a rule that will be ignored.

Keep the tool
    The measurement is still useful: 34 suites do not say what makes them fail, and a reader who wants to spot-check them now has the list instead of the whole directory.

tasks.title: T-AUDIT-32 (P5, low) — AUDITED BY HAND 32/49: TurboMCPNodeType.cpp — 1058 lines, and a note with a written contract that fourteen assignments fill and no caller reads
tasks.description:
Summary
    `TurboMCPNodeType.cpp`, 1058 lines — the largest reader in the tree. One finding, and it is the fifth instance of the pattern this audit keeps finding: a correct idea that is not wired to the place that needs it.

What was found
    An `FString& OutNote` carries a written contract, is filled fourteen times, and is read by nobody. `TurboMCPNodeType.h:140` documents it: "@param OutNote why it could not be built, when it could not. Never empty on failure." `:180` repeats the contract for `SpawnNodeOfType` with one stated exception ("never empty unless Spawned"). The implementation assigns it fourteen times — `:274` "no Blueprint", `:279` "no graph", `:337` "a transient graph for the probe could not be created", plus `:349`, `:358`, `:380`, `:385`, `:440`, `:461`, `:468`, and two `OutNote.Empty()` calls at `:270` and `:376`. A `git grep` for `OutNote` finds only two files in the whole repository: the .cpp with its 14 uses and the .h with 4 (the two declarations and their documentation). No caller passes it and no line reads it — a contract with no counterparty. The implementation does the work the doc promises; the string is discarded.
    The file itself shows where the note belongs: `:469-470` builds the refusal from `ESpawnResult` alone, so the caller is told *that* the spawn failed and never *why*.
    Fix: append the note where the failure is turned into an answer. One line, and the doc already describes what it should say.

Second item, recorded so it is not re-reported
    The transient probe graph. `:334` creates a `UEdGraph` with `RF_Transient`, which invites the "does a read change something?" question, and `:328-333` answers it with the reason: its outer is the Blueprint so a node that walks its outer chain finds one, it is not added to the Blueprint's graph lists, and so nothing in the asset is touched. `:335-338` tests it for null; `:135-137` states the caller's obligation, that the real graph's node count does not change and the caller owns the result. There is no `Modify()`, no `Transaction` and no `MarkPackageDirty` anywhere in the file, so it cannot leave the asset dirty.

Note
    That makes five instances of one pattern at five scales: a `kind` that `KnownKinds` does not accept (`TurboMCPTypes.cpp`), `NormaliseKey` used by two of its four callers (`TurboMCPNodeId.cpp`), a `mutable` documented in `TurboMCPPanelToolRunner.h` that the code replaced with a `const_cast`, a template rule that only 9 of 52 suites follow (`Tools/make-tools-doc.py`), and this one. The defect is the same every time and so is the repair: wire it, or delete it. What must not remain is a contract, a guard, a field or a rule that exists in one place and is consulted in none.

tasks.title: T-AUDIT-UNCOVERED (P3, low) — AUDITED: test-uncovered-tools.py — 176 lines, the best statement of C3 in the audit, and one weak check named
tasks.description:
Summary
    One of the nine suites that names its failure input, and the one that closes the coverage gap. 176 lines, and it contains the best statement of the comment-versus-code problem this audit has read.

Two lessons it records about its own first versions
    1. `:54-61` — the first version asserted the wrong thing and went red on two tools that were right, because it assumed a tool named `<Toolset>Toolset` describes its toolset. Measured, neither does: `LookTurboMCPToolset` lists the live Slate windows a capture could frame, and `PreviewTurboMCPToolset` measures this plugin's help output against the 2000-character budget. So the checks assert what each tool says it does in its own doc comment, which is the only contract it has. A check must assert what the call promises, not what its name suggests.
    2. `:69-73` — assert the output, not the doc comment, because the first version of that check demanded the sentence "it does not capture an image yet" from the header, while `L-CAPTURE` arrived in phase 3 and the caption now reads "look: editing windows, N visible". The header comment is stale and the code is right. A check written from a doc comment tests the comment — and that is the best statement of the underlying problem in this whole audit: the doc and the code diverge, and a test written from the doc validates the doc.

What the suite is for
    `Tools/audit-tool-coverage.py` reads the tool declarations out of the header and the calls out of every suite, and reports the tools that no suite calls. Its first honest run found five, named with their signatures: `EditTurboMCPCompile`, `LookTurboMCPToolset`, `PreviewTurboMCPToolset`, `ReadTurboMCPEditQueue`, `ReadTurboMCPNodeResolve`. A tool that registers and answers nothing when called looks finished in `R-TOOL-INDEX` and in the panel's tool list, and nothing contradicts it — a panel lets a human try a tool, and notices nothing about a tool nobody tried. `:21-27` lists what each check proves before the checks, including that every tool answers rather than returning an empty string, so a reader can see what is and is not covered.

One weak check, named because the card should be honest about the suite it praises
    `:74-75` asserts `look.count("\n") >= 1`, which is true for any multi-line output, including an error message that spans lines. It is not in the cannot-fail class — a single-line answer would fail it — but it is weak, and the suite's own standard says what it needs: a `FAILS ON` line naming the input, for example "fails on: the listing collapsing to one line". The suite names its failures elsewhere, so this is an omission rather than a habit.

Note
    `check-fails-on.py` reports that 34 of 52 suites do not state their failing input. This one does, and it also records the two wrong versions of its own checks — the standard here is high where it is applied.

tasks.title: T-SUITE-01 (P3, medium) — The material suites DO assert the rollback text — but only on the paths the code verifies, which is why 28 unchecked sites are untested
tasks.description:
Summary
    A cross-layer result that reconciles two earlier ones. Ten suites were read, and the material suites do assert the exact rollback text from the C++ — but only on the paths the code itself verifies.

What the suites assert
    `test-material-tidy.py:53` asserts "FAILED: the layout changed the SET OF EXPRESSIONS, so it was ROLLED BACK." `test-material-label-promote.py:71` asserts "was ROLLED BACK." `test-material-blocks.py:72` asserts "FAILED: the edit LOST 1 expression(s) it did not list, so it was ROLLED BACK." All three also state that the fixture is restored on the way in and on the way out and that the restore is asserted (`:34`, `:43`, `:49`), and `test-material-label-promote.py:52` asserts the restore against what the suite did rather than against a count read from the asset — the verify-a-restore-against-the-set rule, already applied in the test layer.
    So the suites do test the rollback, and they assert the exact text the C++ prints.

Why the two earlier results coexist rather than contradict
    The suites assert the rollback on the paths the code verifies — "the set of expressions changed", "lost 1 expression it did not list" — and those paths compare something and report the comparison. The 28 unchecked cancels are on different paths: the ones that fire when `CreateMaterialExpressionEx` returns null, or when a usage node cannot be created. No suite makes an expression creation fail, so no suite exercises those paths.
    So the precise statement is narrower than "the rollback is untested": it is tested where the code measures, and untested where the code only assumes — and those are the twenty-eight sites.

The actionable form
    To close the class, a suite must make an expression creation fail and then assert that the transaction did not commit. `test-material-tidy.py` already has the machinery — `:374` mentions a run interrupted part-way that left the material mid-layout — so the fixture for the failure exists; what is missing is a case where the engine refuses the creation.

And it settles the question the suite rounds raised
    The test layer is not the problem. It tests what the code lets it test. The gap is that the code gives it nothing on twenty-eight paths, because on those paths the code does not check either.

tasks.title: T12 (P1, high) — Atomic multi-asset batch edit
tasks.description:
Architectural decision
    Add a dedicated Preview/Edit batch capability. Do not call existing Edit tools sequentially: each existing writer owns its own transaction, compile, and save, so composition would create multiple undo records and cannot guarantee rollback. The batch owns the only transaction and invokes reusable plan/apply primitives without nested transactions.

Public interface
    Add `PreviewTurboMCPBatchEdit` and `EditTurboMCPBatchEdit` with one `Operations` UTF-8 JSON string. Each operation has an ordered `kind` and the arguments required by that kind (for example `graphRepoint`, `graphSwapCall`, `functionAdd`, or an asset/table operation), plus a stable `id` supplied by the caller. The preview returns the complete ordered plan, affected asset/package set, compile/save phases, and every operation's predicted change.

Required design
    1. Parse and validate the complete operation list before opening a transaction. Reject duplicate IDs, unknown kinds, malformed arguments, and any operation whose plan refuses. Preview performs no writes.
    2. Apply all accepted operations under one `FScopedTransaction` spanning every touched package. Existing writer cores must expose transaction-free plan/apply primitives; wrappers must not call public Edit tools or create nested transactions.
    3. Defer compile and save until every operation has applied. Compile each affected Blueprint once; save each affected package once. Report the ordered compile/save set.
    4. On failure, identify the operation ID and kind, call `FTurboMCPRollback::EndAndUndoActiveTransaction`, and report every operation that had already applied and was rolled back. No partial success response.
    5. After apply, independently read back every operation's target state and compare it with the plan. A failed comparison rolls back and names the mismatch.
    6. The first line is `unchanged` for refusal/rollback and `changed` only after all operations, compiles, saves, and readback checks pass. The result names one undo, one compile phase, one save phase, and the exact rollback scope.

Verification
    First measure whether one transaction can capture modifications in two Blueprint packages and an asset package. Then add a focused four-step batch whose third operation refuses: assert independent reads show no first/second/fourth change, the response names the third operation, and the rollback list is exact. Add a successful multi-asset preview/edit case and assert one compile/save per affected asset.

Rationale
    A batch is a transaction coordinator, not another graph dialect. It must reuse the existing plan cores while moving transaction/compile/save ownership to one outer layer; otherwise the API would claim atomicity it cannot provide.

MEASURED: four consecutive runs this round - test-graph-swap-call.py exit 0 PASS, PASS, PASS, and test-graph-repoint.py exit 0 PASS. But in TWO earlier rounds the swap suite failed `readback preserves the migrated execute link`, both times on the run immediately following a FIXTURE REBUILD.

=== WHY IT STILL MATTERS THOUGH PASSES ARE REPRODUCIBLE ===
A DISAPPEARING DEFECT IS NOT A FIXED ONE. The FAILURE is reproducible too - on the run after a rebuild - and it has now occurred twice. A release cannot ship a suite that fails on its first run and passes on its second, because the first run is the one a fresh checkout performs.
It also cost real rounds: round 22 read it as stale state from earlier refusals, round 39 read it as the swap tool's own un-unified graph resolver, and this round DISPROVED the second of those by running it. That is the ninth mechanism disproved in the graph sequence.

=== THE INSTRUMENT, AND IT IS THE POINT ===
INSTRUMENT THE FAILING RUN, NOT THE PASSING ONES. Concretely: run the suite four times and RECORD WHICH RUN FAILS; then read the state on that run only.
Two candidate readings, NEITHER established:
  * the suite's `rebuild_fixture` + `start-editor` sequence leaves the editor with an asset that has not finished loading or compiling when the first read is taken;
  * the case's first assertion reads state that its own setup invalidates - `rebuild_fixture` is DOCUMENTED to stop the editor and not start it, and test-graph-swap-call.py restarts it, so the first read after a cold start is the one that differs.

=== DO NOT ===
Do not close this because four passes were observed. Do not close it by loosening the check. And do not propose a tenth mechanism from reading code - measure the failing run.

=== ALSO DUE, SEPARATE ===
Six local graph resolvers remain to unify (Comment, GraphAppend, GraphPatch, GraphReplace, GraphStructure x2, GraphSwapCall) onto TurboMCPNodeId::FindGraphByName, plus making the shared resolver report a MULTIPLE MATCH so an ambiguous graph name is refused rather than silently resolved.

tasks.title: S04 / D-008 — an empty graph name: mutators refuse, readers scan explicitly (DECIDED, implementation owed)
tasks.description:
DECIDED BY THE OWNER on 2026-10-17. This is no longer an open question. Evidence: Release/EVIDENCE/S04/compile-rule-restored.md and Release/ARCHITECTURE.md.

=== THE DECISION (D-008) ===
An empty graph name NEVER means "take the first graph". The contract is asymmetric, for the same reason the ambiguity rule is asymmetric:

1. MUTATING tools (Patch, Replace, and every other writer) REFUSE an empty graph name with the code `graph_name_required`, naming the asset and the graphs the caller could have named. A write must not land somewhere the caller did not name.
2. READER and ANALYSIS tools treat an empty graph name as "EVERY graph in the asset". Their report must name each graph scanned and its own counts. A reader that cannot honestly produce an asset-wide answer must refuse rather than answer about one arbitrary graph.
3. No tool may silently resolve to the first graph. `TurboMCPNodeId::FindGraphByName` keeps its current refusal of an empty name; asset-wide scanning is an EXPLICIT iteration at the call site, never an empty-name guess.

=== WHY THIS ANSWER ===
The previous round recorded a used convention and left the choice open: five call sites pass "" and today get the first graph. Taking the first graph is the behaviour an ambiguous node id cannot express, so it cannot survive a release whose identity contract is ARC06. Refusing in readers would break real asset-wide intent (a comment sweep or a dead-node sweep over an asset is a legitimate request), so readers keep the capability but make it explicit and self-describing.

=== IMPLEMENTATION, IN THIS ORDER ===
1. TurboMCPGraphPatch.cpp and TurboMCPGraphReplace.cpp: delete their inline candidate lists and delegate to TurboMCPNodeId::FindGraphByName, then refuse an empty name with `graph_name_required`.
2. Add the explicit all-graphs path to the readers that need it (comment sweep, graph check, dead-node analysis). It iterates the blueprint's graph arrays, labels every section with its graph name, and sets `complete=false` if any graph could not be read.
3. Update the five call sites deliberately, one at a time, choosing refusal or the asset-wide path - never a third meaning:
     test-comments.py:139, :160, :189 (writers: must name a graph)
     test-graph-check.py:205 (reader: asset-wide path)
     test-graph-dead.py:309 (reader: asset-wide path)
4. Cases: an empty name on a writer refuses with `graph_name_required`; an empty name on a reader names every graph and its counts; a named graph still behaves exactly as before.

=== NON-GOALS ===
No change to graph-name semantics for a NON-empty name. No new mutator. The MULTIPLE-MATCH refusal remains a separate item (card f70b1508-3213-4a9d-8c81-07615519e26a closed its specification step; the mutator half exists only in GraphRepoint).

=== ACCEPTANCE ===
G-series identity cases plus the D-008 cases above. A pass requires the writer refusal and the reader's asset-wide report to be observed on a real asset, not inferred from source.
